original_value: Wearable sensors are becoming increasingly popular for complementing classical clinical assessments of gait deficits. The aim of this review is to examine the existing knowledge by systematically reviewing a large number of papers focusing on the use of wearable inertial sensors for the assessment of gait during the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), a widely recognized, simple, non-invasive, low-cost and reproducible exercise test. After a systematic search on PubMed and Scopus databases, two raters evaluated the quality of 28 full-text articles. Then, the available knowledge was summarized regarding study design, subjects enrolled (number of patients and pathological condition, if any, age, male/female ratio), sensor characteristics (type, number, sampling frequency, range) and body placement, 6MWT protocol and extracted parameters. Results were critically discussed to suggest future directions for the use of inertial sensor devices in the clinics.

result.paraphrase: Wearable sensors are gaining popularity as a complement to conventional clinical gait-deficit assessments. This review aims to assess the current evidence by systematically examining many papers on the use of wearable inertial sensors to evaluate gait during the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), a widely recognized exercise test that is simple, non-invasive, low-cost, and reproducible. Following a systematic search of the PubMed and Scopus databases, two raters assessed the quality of 28 full-text articles. The findings were then summarized in terms of study design, enrolled subjects (number of patients and any pathological condition, age, male/female ratio), sensor properties (type, number, sampling frequency, range) and placement on the body, the 6MWT protocol, and the extracted parameters. The results were critically discussed to propose future directions for the clinical use of inertial sensor devices.
